entries.title: Bulls proving rebuilds aren't supposed to look pretty or be pain-free
entries.summary: <p>It’s supposed to be painful.</p><p>On some nights – like Wednesday against Toronto – it can even border on embarrassing.</p><p>That’s what NBA rebuilds are. There has to be a demolition before a rise.</p><p>If there was one criticism to be made about the Bulls’ version of this, however, is it’s two seasons too late. But make no mistake, with 12 games left in the regular season, the rebuild has been flexing its muscles the last 48 hours. On Wednesday, it was a 30-point loss to the Raptors in which there was very little compete from start to finish. A night later against Cleveland, there was a frenzied fourth-quarter comeback that included a 26-8 run to start the final stanza after the Bulls were down as much as 29 points in the game.</p><p>Both very different in feel, but both losses.</p><p>The major difference was there was fight in the 115-110 loss in the second game of the back-to-back.</p><p>The Bulls had a chance to tie the game several times with just over a minute left, but Tre Jones missed a corner three-pointer, Matas Buzelis missed a two-point putback off the miss, and then Leonard Miller messed up a drive off another offensive rebound.</p><p>James Harden has never been one to shy away from a regular-season moment and showed off that star power with 32 seconds left, hitting an 18-footer. No problem, as Jones was at the free throw line a few seconds later but split the pair.</p><p>Down four with 18 seconds left, that left the Bulls no choice but to play the foul game. Like Jones did, Harden split the pair, at least giving the Bulls (28-42) a glimmer of hope. Hope got up and left with 11 seconds left, though, about the same time Matas Buzelis clanked a three-point attempt off the front of the rim.</p><p>Guerschon Yabusele did score on an uncontested layup to pull the home team to within three, but Dennis Schroder iced the game from the stripe.</p><p>“These guys have been great to work with,” Donovan said of the comeback. “They really care, they really want to do well, but we get down tool much. We’ve got to get tougher when things aren’t going our way. They were encouraging each other to just stay with it and we’re going to have to continue to do that.”</p><p>The loss left the Bulls still in the No. 9 seed of the lottery, but again did little to separate them with a Milwaukee team also in a tanking mood.</p><p>Josh Giddey did continue putting his name in the record books, handing out 19 assists to record the most by a Bulls player since Ennis Whatley had 21 on Feb. 23, 1985. Jones led the Bulls with 20 points, while Harden finished with a game-high 36.</p><p>Either way this season ends, however, Donovan was once again asked about the direction the organization is really headed and if he needed clarity from the front office or ownership at some point soon.</p><p>“We’ll do the same thing we’ve always done, kind of sit down at the end of the year,” Donovan said. “We’ve always done that, (executive vice president of basketball operations) Arturas (Karnisovas) and I and (general manager) Marc (Eversley). Obviously, we talk every day about the team. Clearly the biggest thing we’ve gone through is the injuries since the trade deadline, but just trying to get these new guys together, playing together, that’s really where all the focus has been.</p><p>“Certainly, there are guys on expiring contracts, there are restricted contracts, so there will probably be a lot of decisions to make, but we really haven’t talked about those decisions at this point. Going forward we will.”</p>

entries.title: Blackhawks finally beat Wild by finally holding 2-0 lead
entries.summary: <p>It took some help from the goalpost and a potentially goal-saving dive by Alex Vlasic in the final seconds, but the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/blackhawks" target="_blank" >Blackhawks</a> finally beat the Wild.</p><p>The Hawks' 2-1 victory Thursday marked their first in regulation against their <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/blackhawks/2026/03/17/blackhawks-wild-point-total-frank-nazar-louis-crevier" target="_blank" >northern rivals</a> since 2019 and just their second of any sort in 20 meetings during that time span.</p><p>The gap between the two teams had definitely tightened this season — the Hawks took the first three meetings to overtime before ultimately losing all three — but this marked an important step forward.</p><p>"We felt we needed to get one against them before the year ended, so it's good we did that," Connor Bedard told ESPN's John Buccigross afterward.</p><p>It was Bedard's 28th goal of the season — which gave the Hawks a 2-0 edge halfway through the second period — that held up as the game-winner, and it was one of the prettiest of his 28.</p><p>He stripped the puck from Wild veteran Marcus Johansson at the defensive blue line, showed off his increased speed and strength to accelerate quickly for a breakaway and hold off Johansson behind him and then flicked a backhand shot past Jesper Wallstedt.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" > <div class="TweetUrl"> <blockquote class="twitter-tweet"><p lang="en" dir="ltr">CONNOR BEDARD STEALS THE PUCK AND FINDS THE BACK OF THE NET 🗣️ <a href="https://t.co/DkhqCJ6sse">pic.twitter.com/DkhqCJ6sse</a></p>— Sportsnet (@Sportsnet) <a href="https://twitter.com/Sportsnet/status/2034798074946539540?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">March 20, 2026</a></blockquote> <script async src="https://platform.twitter.com/widgets.js" charset="utf-8"></script> </div> </div> </div></div><p>The Hawks are now a respectable 4-2-3 in March with Bedard leading the way; he has 10 points in those nine games. And with 65 points in 55 games on the season, he's just two away from equaling his point total from last season in 27 fewer games.</p><p>Entering Thursday, the Hawks had held a 2-0 lead during the first or second period of 12 games this season — and had incredibly ended up losing seven of those 12 games. It had been remarkable how consistently they've squandered that advantage. </p><p>So it was also important to finally get over that hump in addition to the Minnesota hump.</p><p>The phrasing of "squandering an advantage" suggests their defense (or goaltending) has been to blame, but the bigger problem has been their inability to offensively add to leads — or to reawaken and rebuild the lead after their opponent rallies back.</p><p>In the seven losses — including two prior meetings against the Wild (Nov. 26 at home and Jan. 27 in St. Paul) — the Hawks have scored a grand total of three additional goals after building the 2-0 lead. They've really struggled to regain momentum after having it and then losing it.</p><p>Technically, the Hawks didn't add to their lead Thursday, either. But they at least kept pushing offensively rather than retreating into a shell.</p><p>Although the Wild came extremely close to equalizing during a five-on-three power play halfway through the third period and during the six-on-five situation with the goalie pulled in the final minute, the Hawks also came close to adding an insurance goal — particularly on third-period breakaways by Ryan Greene and Tyler Bertuzzi.</p><p>The Hawks gave up very little during five-on-five play, where were credited with 21 scoring chances compared to the Wild's seven. And goalie Spencer Knight also helped shut the door, saving 28 of 29 shots in his best start since Jan. 19.</p><p>Meanwhile, coach Jeff Blashill returned to an 11-forward, seven-defenseman lineup, which he frequently used in road games earlier this season — appreciating how it allowed him to reduce the workload on his young defensemen and double-shift Bedard with different linemates — but hadn't in a while.</p><p>That lineup construction seemed effective yet again. Nick Lardis still received criminally low ice time (just 8:37), but Ethan Del Mastro's presence as the seventh defenseman added some size and sandpaper in a game that featured plenty of after-the-whistle skirmishes.</p><p>The young Hawks' eagerness to jump into those and stand their ground against a much tougher, older Wild group was good to see.</p>

entries.title: Loyola University student, 18, shot to death in predawn attack at Rogers Park beach
entries.summary: <p>A Loyola University freshman was shot to death early Thursday while she was walking with friends at a Rogers Park beach. </p><p>Sheridan Gorman, 18, was walking with the friends in the 1000 block of West Pratt Boulevard around 1:30 a.m. when a gunman — wearing a face covering — approached them on foot and opened fire in their direction, according to police and Loyola University.</p><p>Gorman’s father, Thomas, was not ready to talk about the shooting Thursday but had one message to share: “Tell everyone to go hug their kids."</p><p>The attack happened on the pier at Tobey Prinz Beach, the university said.</p><p>Gorman was shot in her head and was dead on the scene, police said.</p><p>Gorman, along with three friends, were at the end of a pier when a man in all black clothes and a ski mask jumped from a brush with a weapon, witnesses told police, according to a Chicago Police Department report obtained by the Sun-Times. When the man fired a single shot, they fled in different directions. After Goman’s friends returned from hiding, they found Gorman face down.</p><p>Gorman was shot in her head and was dead at the scene, police said. A single shell casing was found about 40 feet away from her, the report said.</p><p>One man, who didn’t want to be identified out of fear of retribution, said he arrived at the scene about 20 minutes after the incident.</p><p>“One girl is running, and someone was shouting,” the man recalled. “I thought someone was playing with firecrackers.”</p><p>The man said he helped the woman call police, though he didn’t see the alleged suspect.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-650000" entries.title: White Sox' Sam Antonacci returns to spring training, says WBC experience was 'definitely worth it'
entries.summary: <p>GLENDALE, Ariz. — <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox" >White Sox</a> prospect Sam Antonacci knew playing in the World Baseball Classic was a risk.</p><p>It would have been a sensible decision for him to eschew playing for Team Italy in the WBC and continue his torrid spring with the Sox. Antonacci was batting .308/.500/.846 with two homers before he left camp.</p><p>“Definitely worth it,” he said Thursday. “[Italy’s players] all had the same mindset going in, and I definitely made the right choice. Obviously, not having [made my major-league debut] yet or not even making it to Triple-A yet, it was a tough decision in the offseason to make because you want to be here the whole time for spring training. You’re fighting for a spot, and someone who hasn’t played Triple-A yet, it’s probably not the best decision to go out there.</p><p>“But I made [the decision] for moments like [the WBC] and playing in crowds like that to have experience for if I ever were to get called up [because now] I know what it takes and I know what to expect.”</p><p>Antonacci’s numbers in the WBC aren’t anything to write home about — he batted .105/.261/.368. But he burst on the national scene with his heady and frenetic play style.</p><p>In Italy’s 9-1 victory over Team Mexico in Pool B, Mexico’s Jarren Duran hit a fly ball to left-center field with Joey Ortiz on first base. Ortiz ran with the pitch, and Antonacci, playing shortstop, perfectly executed a deke, lunging toward second base as if the ball had been hit his way and trickled into the outfield. Ortiz continued running toward third and was eventually doubled up.</p><p>In a two-week span, Antonacci demonstrated the contact skills and all-out style that have endeared him to the Sox’ organization.</p><p>Though the experience will undoubtedly benefit Antonacci and catcher Kyle Teel, who also played on Team Italy, the Sox were burned when Teel went down with a strained hamstring in Italy’s 8-6 victory against Team USA. Though Antonacci didn’t get hurt, his needless headfirst dive into first base during the semifinal loss to Team Venezuela surely had Sox officials holding their breath.</p><p>“When you are talking about two players who get after it like they do, sometimes it can come at risk,” general manager Chris Getz said. “But I am proud of how those guys have been representing the organization, and I’m really happy for those guys.”</p><p>Antonacci is starting the season in the minors. He batted .291/.433/.409 in 116 games across three affiliate levels last season, ultimately finishing in Double-A Birmingham.</p><p>Though he played shortstop for Italy — and has played the position throughout the minors — he could end up as a utility player as the Sox look to take advantage of his impressive contact skills. Before he left, Antonacci even started to showcase some power, which hasn’t been a part of his game. He said that he started to chase homers after having some success and had to dial it back. As long as Antonacci continues producing, he’ll force his way to the majors sooner than later.</p><p>“I’ve kind of done a good job of letting the power come to me,” Antonacci said. -“Towards the end of [his first stint in spring training], my swing’s gotten a little bit bigger after seeing a couple of homers go over, maybe [was] trying to do too much.</p><p>“I need to understand that it’ll come on its own and I don’t need to be searching for that and continue to take my short swing and the power will come.”</p><div class="PageListL" data-module data-hide-authors="true" entries.title: Still a lot of 'What could have been' with former Bull Lonzo Ball
entries.summary: <p>This was supposed to be the part of the season in which Lonzo Ball was unleashed.</p><p>That plan was made very public by Kenny Atkinson way back in October, as the Cleveland coach had Ball’s season mapped out.</p><p>“Really with (Ball), more than anyone, our goal with him is to have him ready for the playoffs,” Atkinson said then. “There’s a reason this guy was a second overall pick in our league. He’s one of those guys that makes other players better, which is a coach’s dream, right?”</p><p>A dream until it’s not.</p><p>Ball never looked right after the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bulls" >Bulls</a> traded him to Cleveland for Isaac Okoro last offseason, leaving the Cavs no choice but to finally move off of him with a trade to Utah in February. The Jazz promptly waived him as he now sits at home hoping to get another chance in the NBA.</p><p>“I loved him as a player and a guy, and he was so cerebral,” Bulls coach Billy Donovan said of Ball on Thursday, reflecting on the frequently-injured point guard. “He was so selfless, that’s really one of the things I admired. To see him have to go through what he went through, to fight to get back, see what he’s going through now, that’s tough for me because it’s almost like what could have been, how good could he have been?”</p><p>The big what if with Ball after a serious knee injury back in 2022 cost him over two-and-a-half seasons. Even when he returned, he only showed glimpses of the player he was before the knee betrayed him.</p><p>As for Okoro, he has given the Bulls solid wing defense and is actually one of the few roster moves by Arturas Karnisovas that the executive vice president can call a win.</p><p>Okoro, who has been sidelined for over a week with a sore knee, is signed through next season and has impressed Donovan in multiple ways.</p><p>“He was always a good defensive player in college, but he became this guys that can guard one through four.” Donovan said. “The other part with him that stands out with me is he’s really, really smart. He knows how to play with good players, he knows how to play in screening action with good players. He’s incredibly unselfish in terms of he’s not trying to hunt shots, trying to hunt points. When you talk to him it’s never about him, it’s always about the team and what he has to do to help the team. He looks at the group, looks at the team and thinks, ‘OK, what can I do to help enhance the group.’ “</p><p></p><h3><b>Eye test</b></h3><p></p><p>Because he’s getting consistent minutes for really the first time in his NBA career, guard Rob Dillingham said he’s also starting to build chemistry up with his newer teammates.</p><p>“That feels great because people might not look at me as your average point guard, but I honestly feel like I can run a team,” Dillingham said. “I might not be the modern day regular point guard out there running the team, but I feel like I can grow in that, add that in playing my game. It will take some time. Building that chemistry definitely helps, especially when it comes to making plays for my team.”</p><p></p><h3><b>Back-to-sitting</b></h3><p></p><p>With the Bulls having a back-to-back and Jalen Smith feeling some tightness in the calf that’s sidelined him several games this season, the big man was given Thursday’s game off to rest the injury.</p><p>The Bulls don’t play again until Monday, so that entries.summary: <p>When Andre Ruddock was born, doctors told his family they didn't think he would live.</p><p>Ruddock had health problems because his mother was addicted to heroin when she was pregnant with him. </p><p>“Obviously, I made it, but that's how I ended up as a ward of the state in the Department of Children and Family Services,” said Ruddock, 49, who grew up on the South Side.</p><p>He doesn’t see his upbringing as a sad story. He got to interact with many different people from diverse backgrounds. But he does think he became a product of the negative parts of his environment.</p><p>Ruddock was incarcerated at age 16 and spent 28 years in prison.</p><p>As his release date approached after spending decades in prison, he faced the difficult reality of having no place to live.</p><p>“I would be homeless upon my release. I didn't really know where I was going to go,” he said. “My family had kind of dissipated to the point where I knew I wouldn't be able to live with any of them.”</p><p>When was released, Ruddock was told he had been approved for a rental assistance program through the Illinois Housing Development Authority's reentry rental assistance program that Home for Good aims to build upon.</p><p>“At that time, I didn’t know what it was. I was just happy I had somewhere to go," he said. "I grew up in prison, so I’m 44 years old now. That’s my first time in the world as an adult. I left as a child. So I definitely never owned anything. To have my own set of keys was a big deal. That was a gigantic thing.”</p><p>That is why Ruddock is advocating for legislation proposed by the Home for Good Coalition to increase housing and support services for people like him returning from prison.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-cb0000" name="image-cb0000"></a> <picture class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Andre Ruddock, founder of Returning Citizens in Memory of Henry Dee, speaks Thursday during a Home for Good Coalition rally at the National Public Housing Museum.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Candace Dane Chambers/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>The group is made up of Illinois advocacy organizations working toward expansion of housing and support services for people who have spent time in prison.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://ilga.gov/Documents/legislation/104/SB/10400SB4162.htm" target="_blank" ><u>Illinois Senate Bill 4162</u></a> is a bipartisan proposal that aims to expand Home for Good as a statewide coordinated program helping people released from prison by providing them with rental assistance, job training, furniture, child care, food and other reentry resources.</p><p>Proponents of the bill believe the law will strengthen the state and local economy and save taxpayers money.</p><p>State Sen. Lakesia Collins, (D-Chicago), said this is a personal issue. Her father was in and out of the prison system, and she saw firsthand how powerful second chances are.</p><p>“The more that we can do to stabilize people who are justice-involved, the better we are as a state,” Collins said. “You spend more money with them going into prison every single day, with food, housing them and the rent that you have to pay for a lot of these buildings.”</p><p>Collins believes that money instead can go to people recently released from prison so they can get a job and give back to society. She said this could save the state money and allow funds to be redirected to other priorities, such as education.</p><p>State Sen. Adriane Johnson (D-Buffalo Grove) is sponsoring the plan. If it passes committee, it will proceed to the floor for a vote, and if it receives enough support, it will move to the House.</p><p>“I'll be someone who's voting yes for it,” Collins said.</p><p>To garner more support, the Home for Good Coalition held a rally to promote the legislation at the National Public Housing Museum on Thursday.</p><p>Speakers included Ahmadou Dramé, director of the Illinois Justice Project; Joakim Noah, former Chicago Bulls All-Star and co-founder of Noah’s Arc Foundation; and Collins, among others.</p><p>Noah said he attended the rally to show his support for reentry and community stability through housing and community programs. He retired from professional basketball five years ago and has continued working with at-risk children through his Noah’s Arc Foundation. Noah said advocating for Home for Good legislation aligns with his organization’s mission to promote violence prevention and community engagement.</p><p>“I thank God that we can do this work, and being of service has given me so much purpose,” Noah said. “I really feel like this is who I am, and it's been a constant in my life for a long time. entries.title: Ten years later, Cubs would love to duplicate championship success
entries.summary: <p>MESA, Ariz. — It has been 10 years already since the Cubs won a World Series.</p><p>Seems like it’s about time for another one.</p><p>Never mind that the organization once known as baseball’s lovable losers took 108 years to win one in 2016, its first since 1908. These 2026 Cubs can dream big again without being scoffed at.</p><p>But this outfit is a decade removed from the squad led by Anthony Rizzo, Kris Bryant, Jake Arrieta and Jon Lester that made front-page news when it celebrated a Game 7 victory Nov. 2, 2016, in Cleveland.</p><p>Cubs 2026 Opening Day starter Matthew Boyd was trying (and mostly failing) to beat Cleveland and watching closely as a member of a good Tigers team in ’16, but many of today’s Cubs were teenagers at the time and didn’t care all that much.</p><p>Matt Shaw was almost 15.</p><p>“I wasn’t a Cubs fan; I was a Red Sox fan, so I was like, ‘Whatever,’ ’’ Shaw said.</p><p>“To be honest, I didn’t really watch,” said right-hander Porter Hodge, also a Red Sox fan at the time.</p><p>“But I remember the iconic photo of Rizzo getting the last out [at first base on a slip-sliding throw from Bryant at third], stuff like that,” Shaw said. “I don’t remember being excited about it, though, to be honest.”</p><p>Nico Hoerner had no idea he’d be a Cub when he watched it from his dorm at Stanford.</p><p>“It was my sophomore year,” Hoerner said. “I was a baseball fan. It was kind of cool.”</p><p>How cool would it be to be in the middle of a dogpile at Wrigley Field this fall?</p><p>“Oh, my gosh,” Boyd said. “Even when we were in the wild card and Division Series last year, it was unbelievable. Talk to any guy here, they have a chills moment of what it felt like. Those home games, the fans chanting, ‘Freddy,’ when [Brewers ace] Freddy Peralta was pitching, unbelievable. We were really blessed to be there.”</p><p>Players, fans, ballpark workers and media inside Wrigley during the Cubs’ 2016 run won’t forget the enormous levels of energy and noise at every game. The Cubs are celebrating their 150th anniversary as a National League franchise but will stir 2016 memories when they also observe the 10-year anniversary this season.</p><p>A painted chalk wall memorializing fan inscriptions from the World Series celebration will be added to the left-field Budweiser bleacher concourse, a permanent monument will be installed to honor the Cubs’ three championship teams and a July 18 dedication ceremony with players and fans will celebrate the 2016 team.</p><p>Rizzo is throwing out the ceremonial first pitch Opening Day, moments before Boyd throws the first pitch that counts for 2026.</p><p>While with the Tigers in 2016, Boyd followed the Cubs closely because his late grandfather was born in Chicago and was a huge Cubs fan who said watching them win the World Series was one of the happiest moments of his life.</p><p>His grandfather wasn’t alone in that regard.</p><p>“It was cool for baseball,” Boyd said.</p><p>“Having success in Chicago would be something because the fan base is so ‘we love the Cubbies.’ It was something to be a part of last year, just getting a taste of the postseason, seeing the excitement level up every time we moved up with the next win.</p><p>“And that was only the DS; imagine what it would be like in the NL Championship Series and World Series.”</p><p>“It’s not a normal place, in the best way possible,” Hoerner said. “We got a glance at that last year, even just winning a first-round series against the Padres.”</p><p>Losing Game 5 might somehow pay off this season. The Cubs got swept by the Mets in the 2015 NLCS and came back feeding off the disappointment.</p><p>“There are two sides of having success but falling short,” Hoerner said. “You can draw positives from it. And it’s nice to have a group that’s held together pretty well from one year to the next.”<br></p>

entries.title: David Mirkovic leads No. 3 Illinois to 105-70 rout of No. 14 Penn
entries.summary: <p>GREENVILLE, S.C. — David Mirkovic had 29 points and 17 rebounds, and No. 3 seed Illinois dominated No. 14 seed Penn 105-70 on Thursday night in the first round of the NCAA Tournament.</p><p>Keaton Wagler added 18 points, seven assists and seven rebounds for the Fighting Illini (25-8), who moved on to face No. 11 VCU in the second round on Saturday.</p><p>Kylan Boswell had 13 points, while Ben Humrichous and Tomislav Ivisic each chipped in with 12 as Illinois shot 50% from the field, made 15 3-pointers and outrebounded the much smaller Quakers 48-25.</p><p>Michael Zanoni finished with 20 points on 9-of-18 shooting for Penn (18-12), the Ivy League champion.</p><p>TJ Power, who scored 44 points in the Quakers' overtime win over Yale that got them into the tournament, finished with six points on 2-of-8 shooting in 30 minutes after missing the previous two practices with an illness that left his status for the game uncertain.</p><p>Illinois coach Brad Underwood said Wagler did a “phenomenal" job guarding Power.</p><p>“He gave up the last 3 before the end of the half (to Power), which I wasn’t very happy with, but his touches were very hard,” Underwood said.</p><p>Mirkovic set the tone for Illinois with a huge first half, as his 17 points and 10 rebounds helped the Fighting Illini build a 40-30 lead.</p><p>“He was the best player on the court tonight, especially in the first half, his physicality,” Underwood said. “Ten rebounds in a half and 17 points. Again, we talk about (rebounds) being our daily vitamins and we had a 28-14 advantage at half. Then it was just delivering body blows.”</p><p>Illinois continued to grab rebound after rebound and stretched the lead to 23 with 10 minutes remaining after Mirkovic came up with a steal and fed Zvonimir Ivisic for a transition alley-oop dunk.</p><p>“Their size was tough to contend with,” Penn guard Cam Thrower said.</p><p>Mirkovic's 17 rebounds where a school tournament record. He said the ball was finding him like a magnet on the offensive glass.</p><p>“That’s what I do every day, even practices,” Mirkovic said. “I just crash the board trying to bring that physicality. I was crashing and I got a lot of easy points on the rim.”</p><p><b>Wagler: Mirkovic is nation's most overlooked freshman</b></p><p>There has been plenty made about the talent of this year's freshman class that includes Duke's Cameron Boozer, Kansas' Darryn Peterson and BYU's AJ Dybantsa.</p><p>Wagler, a second-team Associated Press All-American as a freshman, believes Mirkovic deserves to be mentioned in that class.</p><p>“All year he’s been one of the best freshmen in the country,” Wagler said. “With this loaded freshman class we have, he’s been overshadowed a bit. He rebounds, plays physical, plays hard all the time. I think tonight he just showed what he’s capable of.”</p><p><b>Fran McCaffrey said AJ Power wasn't 100% healthy</b></p><p>Penn coach Fran McCaffrey said Power had “four of five IVs” before the game but simply “wasn't himself” after battling an illness.</p><p>But he credited him for battling through and playing the entire first half.</p><p>“That is one tough kid there,” McCaffrey said. “I love him. He tried. He was sick for two days. We thought he was going to get better. ... But you could tell, in particular on the glass, because he’s an elite rebounder, that he didn’t have quite the energy or the explosion that he normally does."</p><p><b>Penn players say thank you to followers</b></p><p>After the game the Penn players walked in unison over toward their fans and applauded them. Some tugged at their jerseys and waved and others blew kisses. The fans applauded and cheered back, with one yelling, “Next year, boys!”</p><p><b>Up next</b></p><p>Illinois beat VCU 62-46 in the only meeting between the schools in 2016.<br></p>

entries.summary: <p>In Sunday’s sports section, I found it dismaying to encounter the men’s and women’s NCAA brackets on facing pages: the men’s in bold, dynamic color and the women’s diminished in sad gray.</p><p>In these times when the differences between men and women, white and nonwhite, majority and minority are so amplified, equal treatment of the brackets should have been a no-brainer.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-floatRight> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-c80000" name="image-c80000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/b0c7a7e/2147483647/strip/true/crop/960x539+0+59/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F91%2Fe4%2F4dd8779d4e8193ff2c9520150d67%2Fimg-5612.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/6fd6ff9/2147483647/strip/true/crop/960x539+0+59/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F91%2Fe4%2F4dd8779d4e8193ff2c9520150d67%2Fimg-5612.jpg 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/c597b88/2147483647/strip/true/crop/960x539+0+59/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F91%2Fe4%2F4dd8779d4e8193ff2c9520150d67%2Fimg-5612.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="A tabloid style newspaper opened. Two pages can be seen with chartlight graphics. " srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/c597b88/2147483647/strip/true/crop/960x539+0+59/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F91%2Fe4%2F4dd8779d4e8193ff2c9520150d67%2Fimg-5612.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/df5e01b/2147483647/strip/true/crop/960x539+0+59/resize/980x550!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F91%2Fe4%2F4dd8779d4e8193ff2c9520150d67%2Fimg-5612.jpg 2x" width="490" height="275" data-src="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/c597b88/2147483647/strip/true/crop/960x539+0+59/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F91%2Fe4%2F4dd8779d4e8193ff2c9520150d67%2Fimg-5612.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" > </picture> <div class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>The men’s and women’s NCAA brackets on facing pages in Sunday’s Sun-Times.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Provided </p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>I understand the pages of the paper alternate between color and black and white. You can’t change that, and at least both brackets were the same size. It’s clear no one meant any insult. It was just a practical business decision based on the pages and inks available. However, all we have to do is turn back to Scoop Jackson’s column that same day to see <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/sports/2026/03/14/wbc-world-baseball-classic-team-usa-black-players-aaron-judge-byron-buxton-mark-derosa" >business decisions</a> used as license to discriminate in sports.</p><p>We can do better. There was no way to render the women’s bracket in color because it was on a page printed with only black ink. But there’s nothing that says the men’s bracket had to use colors of ink available on its page. Next time, send cyan, magenta and yellow to the bench in the name of equality.</p><p><i>Todd Schultz, St. Joseph, Michigan</i></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-980000" name="module-980000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>Give us your take</h3><br>Send letters to the editor to <a class="Link" href="mailto:letters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >letters@suntimes.com</a>. Letters should be a maximum of approximately 375 words.</div> </div><p></p><h3>Misplaced priorities in the U.S. </h3><h3></h3><p>WBEZ's Chip Mitchell's story of <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/real-estate/2026/03/16/legion-park-chicago-tent-encampment-homeless-unhoused-fire" >Carmen Laude</a> in Tuesday’s Sun-Times was tragic. How can we be the richest country in the world and have people who worked lose their home over medical debt?</p><p>The story also made me break out my calculator. If we took the <a class="Link" href="https://time.com/article/2026/03/16/what-us-spending-on-the-war-in-iran-could-fund-instead/" target="_blank" >$1 billion a day</a> we are spending doing whatever it is we are doing in Iran and distributed it to our nation’s <a class="Link" href="https://endhomelessness.org/state-of-homelessness/" target="_blank" >770,000 homeless</a>, we could pay them in a day $1,300 — what it takes them to have a home for a month.</p><p>Our priorities in this country are wack. The next time someone tells you we are a Christian nation, I suggest you laugh in their face.</p><p><i>Don Anderson, Oak Park</i> </p><h3>Haunting thoughts </h3><p>I don't believe in ghosts, but it seems the Jeffrey Epstein haunting is so formidable, it compelled us to engage in a protracted war.</p><p><i>Larry Niemi, Loop</i></p><h3>Bone to pick </h3> <p>President Donald Trump has said that the Iran war will be over <a class="Link" href="https://www.politico.com/news/2026/03/13/trump-iran-war-ending-timeline-00828138" target="_blank" >“when I feel it in my bones.”</a> Does this include his <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2017/10/23/18331262/mccain-issues-veiled-criticism-of-trump-s-vietnam-deferment" >bone spurs</a> that prevented him from serving [in the military]?</p><p><i>Dennis Fitzgerald, Melbourne, Australia</i></p><h3>Next steps?</h3><p>As Donald J. Trump has done all his life, will he walk away from the U. S. presidency as he is prone to do in any situation where he does not get his way?</p><p><i>Eileen Hughes, Near North Side</i> <br></p>

entries.title: Dear Abby: Parents continue to ignore older son's request
entries.summary: <p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> I am in my late 30s. I live halfway across the country from my parents and don't have the best relationship with them. I also have a brother four years younger from whom I have been estranged for 20 years. He lives in the same city as my parents.</p><p>My problem is, if I visit, my parents (especially my mom) will tell my brother and invite him over. I don't like my brother and don't want to see him. I will not reconcile with him because he did some horrible things to me 20 years ago for which I can never forgive him.</p><p>With my parents, things don't get through to them unless I take drastic measures. How can I convey my desire not to see him? My plan would be to tell them they must agree not to invite him to their house while I'm there — and if they can't respect my wishes, I simply won't see them.</p><p>I'm not worried about being without lodging because I have friends I can stay with there. In fact, I have made several trips to that city without visiting my parents. What is your perspective on how I can "lay down the law" and enforce it? — <i>INDEPENDENT IN MASSACHUSETTS</i></p><p><b>DEAR INDEPENDENT:</b> Have an honest conversation with your parents. Explain what happened between you and your brother. Emphasize that you do not wish to see him again — ever. Tell them you would like to visit them, but you do not want your brother to be informed or invited over while you are there. If they cannot agree, explain (without hostility) that you will skip the visit. This is not "laying down the law"; it is creating a boundary.</p><p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> My wife and I welcomed our third child into the world six months ago. Since then, my wife has been diagnosed with postpartum depression and has cheated on me multiple times. She has now moved out. She is dating a woman and wants a divorce.</p><p>Despite all of this, I have forgiven her, and I still love her. Her behavior is negatively affecting our other children, but she refuses to acknowledge its impact and won't listen to me or talk to me about it. She refuses to go to counseling and acts like everything is my fault. How should I handle this? — <i>DISTRAUGHT HUSBAND IN PENNSYLVANIA</i></p><p><b>DEAR HUSBAND:</b> If you had no hint that your wife was bisexual before this, it must have been a shock. As I see it, there are two ways to handle this. The first would be to talk with a licensed mental health professional and ask if that person can give you some insight into whether postpartum has caused your wife's behavior. None of this is your fault, and it may not be your wife's fault either.</p><p>The second way is to start interviewing lawyers who specialize in family law. While you can't force your wife to stay married to you, you can make sure your children spend as much time with their father as possible.</p><p><i>Dear Abby is written by Abigail Van Buren, also known as Jeanne Phillips, and was founded by her mother, Pauline Phillips. Contact Dear Abby at www.DearAbby.com or P.O. Box 69440, Los Angeles, CA 90069.</i></p><p>For an excellent guide to becoming a better conversationalist and a more sociable person, order "How to Be Popular." Send your name and mailing address, plus check or money order for $8 (U.S. funds), to: Dear Abby, Popularity Booklet, P.O. Box 446, Kings Mills, OH 45034-0446. (Shipping and handling are included in the price.)</p>

entries.title: United Airlines' fight for supremacy at O'Hare is terrible for travelers
entries.summary: <p>Brace yourself if you're flying through O'Hare Airport this summer. Depending on the Federal Aviation Administration's decisions over the coming weeks, fewer choices, higher fares and more disruption are likely headed your way — and not entirely by accident. </p><p>The agency has been <a class="Link" href="https://www.reuters.com/world/us/faa-plans-reduce-flights-chicago-ohare-citing-boost-schedules-2026-02-27/" target="_blank" >forced to step in</a> ahead of the busy summer season to address the gap between scheduled flights and the capacity the airport is actually equipped to handle. For the millions of passengers who rely on O'Hare every year, the FAA’s decision will not be an abstraction. It could mean a missed connection, a canceled trip or a fare that suddenly costs twice what it did last year.</p><p>This crisis didn't happen on its own. It was triggered, and arguably even engineered, by United Airlines’ deliberate strategy to gain more control of the airport. Airlines have over-scheduled O'Hare for this upcoming summer, <a class="Link" href="https://www.cbsnews.com/chicago/news/faa-ohare-flight-reductions-united-american-airlines/" target="_blank" >projecting</a> more than 3,000 daily operations, up from around 2,680 during peak days last year. The FAA determined that the airport's infrastructure and air traffic control staffing cannot safely support that volume — and Chicago is all too familiar with why that can’t stand. During the 2025 government shutdown, controller shortages triggered ground stops and <a class="Link" href="https://abc7chicago.com/post/national-airspace-system-status-flight-cancellations-chicagos-ohare-midway-airports-begin-faa-reduces-capacity/18124735/" target="_blank" >dozens of daily cancellations</a> at O'Hare alone.</p><p>Knowing this, why are airlines scheduling so far beyond what the airport can handle?</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-270000" name="module-270000"></a> <div class="RichTextSidebarModule-title">Commentary bug</div> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h2>Commentary</h2></div> </div><p>In the case of United Airlines, the answer is uncomfortable, but the airline's own leadership has made the strategy clear: Chaos is fine, as long as the fix hurts competitors more. United is planning 750 daily departures from O'Hare this summer, an <a class="Link" href="https://www.chicagobusiness.com/airlines-airports/united-airlines-plans-record-number-ohare-flights" target="_blank" >increase of more than 30%</a>, according to Crain's Chicago Business. These <a class="Link" href="https://www.chicagotribune.com/2026/03/04/editorial-united-american-airlines-ohare-airport-faa-summer-travel/" target="_blank" >aren’t in-demand routes</a> launched to help travelers. They are designed to exploit O'Hare's gate assignment policy, which allocates gates based solely on flights scheduled — a "use it or lose it" approach. </p><p>On a January earnings call, United CEO Scott Kirby <a class="Link" href="https://thepointsguy.com/news/united-american-airlines-chicago-ohare-hub-line-in-sand/" target="_blank" >declared</a>: "We're not going to allow them [American Airlines] to win a single gate at our expense in 2026." His chief financial officer <a class="Link" href="https://www.businessinsider.com/united-airlines-cfo-belittles-american-airlines-in-fight-for-chicago-2026-2" target="_blank" >called</a> American's presence at O'Hare temporary, predicting that "everybody is switching from American to United."</p><h3>Turf war</h3><p>This is not a passenger service strategy. This is a land grab. United Airlines is adding <a class="Link" href="https://www.travelweekly.com/Travel-News/Airline-News/United-new-routes-competitive-surge-OHare" target="_blank" >dozens</a> of low-demand flights, knowing that it can roll them back once the FAA mandates cuts and still come out ahead of other carriers forced to cancel their own valuable flights. The airline has also been buying up gates, including<a class="Link" href="https://simpleflying.com/why-united-paid-30m-for-gates-its-ceo-swore-he-didnt-want/" target="_blank" > paying $30 million for Spirit Airlines’ gates</a> that it previously claimed were not of interest. With its scheduling surge, United is burning through O'Hare's finite capacity not to better serve travelers but to crowd out rivals.</p><p>Why does this matter beyond a corporate turf war? Because O'Hare is one of the last major U.S. airports where two legacy carriers genuinely compete through dual hubs, and that competition directly benefits passengers. Fares stay lower. Service improves. Travelers have real choices.</p><p>American Airlines may not admit it, but with its comparatively smaller hub, it has invested in upgrading its Chicago product precisely because competition demands it.</p><p>The warning signs of a less competitive O'Hare are already visible. Southwest is already <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/transportation/2026/03/13/southwest-airlines-ohare" target="_blank" >planning to exit the airport</a>. As United crowds out rivals, options disappear and travelers lose leverage. A United near-monopoly wouldn't just be bad for Chicago, it would be bad for the millions of connecting passengers who pass through O'Hare every year.</p><p>None of this lets the FAA and Congress off the hook. Flight caps are a band-aid, not a cure, and a resilient solution — at O’Hare, and beyond — means more work ahead. Our air traffic control system still runs on decades-old technology despite significant public investment over the past decade. Thousands of controller positions remain unfilled. Sens. Tammy Duckworth and Dick Durbin of Illinois have rightly <a class="Link" href="https://www.duckworth.senate.gov/news/press-releases/duckworth-durbin-call-for-greater-faa-investment-and-efficiency-at-chicago-ohare-airport" target="_blank" >urged</a> the FAA to fix O'Hare's staffing crisis beyond addressing flight schedules, but so far the urgency hasn't matched the rhetoric. U.S. travelers pay more than 20% of their ticket price in taxes and fees. They are entitled to a modern, functioning system in return.</p><h3>Testing travelers’ patience</h3><p>The FAA and Department of Transportation must examine whether United's scheduling practices constitute anti-competitive manipulation of gate allocation rules. Congress must treat air traffic control modernization as the national infrastructure emergency it is. Chicago and federal regulators must recognize that protecting O'Hare's dual-hub status is consumer protection, and ensure plans for flight cuts don’t ultimately reward anti-competitive behavior. And any flight reductions this summer must come with enforceable passenger protections: transparent rebooking, no fare-gouging and clear communication to affected travelers.</p><p>O'Hare's crisis is a microcosm of everything wrong in U.S. aviation: underinvestment in infrastructure, airlines that prioritize dominance over service, and regulators perpetually playing catch-up. Travelers have been patient through shutdowns, staffing crises and a capacity crunch that was foreseeable and deliberately manufactured.</p><p>The FAA has the authority to act. Congress has the tools. What has been missing for too long is the will to put travelers first. That's what every passenger flying through O'Hare this summer deserves.</p><p><i>Charlie Leocha is president and co-founder of the consumer advocacy group Travelers United.</i></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-ce0000" name="module-ce0000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody">Send letters to <a class="Link" href="mailto:letters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >letters@suntimes.com</a>. More about <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/submitting-opinion-and-letters" >how to submit here</a>.</div> </div><p></p>

entries.title: Government shutdowns, long airport lines have become the new normal
entries.summary: <p>If you’ve ever traveled to France, chances are you’ve come up against this all-too-common phenomenon. You get to the train station and, without warning, your train is out of service. Or a restaurant is oddly closed during regular business hours.</p><p>"C’est la grève," you may hear from a local, accompanied by a shrug. It’s the strike.</p><p>There’s a joke in France about its time-honored tradition of labor protests: A tourist asks a waiter what the signs are about at a protest across the street. The waiter hardly looks up and simply says, "Thursday."</p><p>Strikes, protests, work stoppages and closures are so frequent in France, there are multiple apps and websites devoted to letting locals and tourists alike know what will be open and what will be closed, and those in the know check daily.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-d80000" name="module-d80000"></a> <div class="RichTextSidebarModule-title">Columnist </div> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody">Columnist</div> </div><p>A strike today at schools in Dijon, Lyon and Rennes; an ongoing transport strike in Rouen; closures at the Louvre. <a class="Link" href="https://www.cestlagreve.fr/" target="_blank" >One site</a> promises: "Thanks to our service, unexpected problems are a thing of the past. You’ll no longer be stuck waiting for your train, and you can plan a backup solution!"</p><p>Americans may hear this and smugly scoff at a society that’s turned such dysfunction into a revered art form. But our pride is increasingly undeserved.</p><p>Last week I flew between Newark and Austin. As you may have seen on the news, the security lines were hours long and, in some cases, snaked out the airport doors and onto the street.</p><p>This wasn’t because of a protest or a strike, however, but yet another government shutdown, the third in just six months.</p><p>Starting in October last year and lasting for 43 days, we endured the longest shutdown in U.S. history due to an impasse over Affordable Care Act subsidies. Then, earlier this year, a partial shutdown over delays in a funding package linked to immigration. And now, going on more than a month, we’re in another partial shutdown over Department of Homeland Security funding.</p><p>The <a class="Link" href="https://www.nytimes.com/2026/03/16/travel/tsa-airport-delays-shutdown.html" target="_blank" >shutdown</a> has meant about 50,000 Transportation Security Administration officers have been working without pay. Many have picked up second jobs, while others are calling in sick and more than 300 have simply quit.</p><p>Acting Deputy TSA Administrator Adam Stahl says we’re rapidly approaching a breaking point:</p><p>“If the call rate does climb," <a class="Link" href="https://www.cbsnews.com/news/tsa-airports-could-shut-down-officer-call-out-rate-climbs/" target="_blank" >he said</a> of agents calling out of work, "there could be scenarios where we may have to shut down airports. This is a serious situation."</p><p>You’d think Congress would want to fix this quickly in an election year, but all evidence points to the contrary. Republicans and Democrats remain in a stalemate over DHS funding, with both parties blaming each other and using strikingly similar language to do so.</p><p>"Democrats need to end their political posturing, stop using our TSA agents as political pawns, and fully fund DHS," <a class="Link" href="https://www.cnn.com/2026/03/19/us/tsa-political-impacts" target="_blank" >said</a> Sen. Katie Britt, R-Ala.</p><p>Sen. Raphael Warnock, D-Ga., <a class="Link" href="https://www.youtube.com/shorts/nClkqs020bw" target="_blank" >said</a>, "I think it’s simply wrong for my Republican colleagues to use these hard-working Americans as leverage, as pawns, in what they are presenting as a false choice to the American people."</p><p>But while both parties finger-point, all the average American sees is a dysfunctional government getting more dysfunctional by the day, with basic pursuits — like air travel — feeling more like capricious and unreliable luxuries.</p><p>While inching through security in Austin, someone asked me what the lines were about. "The shutdown," I said. He didn’t even know we were in one again.</p><p>We deserve better from our government. But if this is just our new normal — where on any given day we’re left wondering what parts of our government are open and running — we may, like the French, need to get ourselves an app for that.</p><p><i>S.E. Cupp is the host of “S.E. Cupp Unfiltered” on CNN.</i></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-8f0000" name="module-8f0000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody">Send letters to <a class="Link" href="mailto:letters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >letters@suntimes.com</a>. More about <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/submitting-opinion-and-letters" >how to submit here</a>.</div> </div><p></p>

entries.title: Definition of a company man? Calbert Wright, who’s been working at Ford’s Chicago Heights plant since 1963
entries.summary: <p>He didn't think he'd stick around.</p><p>When Calbert Wright began work at the Ford Motor Company's Chicago Stamping Plant in Chicago Heights in 1963, the factory was a noisy, smelly, smoky hellscape with a leaky roof. </p><p>And it was hot: 100 degrees on the production line.</p><p>"Ooo," Wright said. "No fans. Water fountains were rare, very rare."</p><p>Plus Black workers such as himself were given the hardest duties.</p><p>"The first month, I didn't like it," remembers Wright, 85, "I said, 'I'm not going to stay here'. They had us stacking steel. We couldn't touch no presses. All we could do is stack stock. They were trying to work us like Hebrew slaves."</p><p>But stay he did.</p><p>When Wright began work at the age of 23 at Ford, John F. Kennedy was president. Henry Ford still ran the business — albeit Henry Ford II, grandson of the man who founded the automobile manufacturer in 1903.</p><p>That means Wright, who prowls the floor today checking that workers on the line have enough parts to keep the robots busy — and takes their place when they go on bathroom breaks — has worked for Ford a little more than half the 123 years since the company sold its first car, a two-cylinder, two-passenger Model A, in red, the only color available, for $850 to Ernest Pfennig, a dentist on Clybourn Avenue.</p><p>Wright had come up from Mississippi when he was 11, and his voice is rich with Southern drawl. He had an uncle at Ford's Torrence Avenue assembly plant, and got a job at Chicago Stamping.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-fe0000" name="image-fe0000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/9a360cb/2147483647/strip/true/crop/4927x2765+0+260/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F96%2Fc8%2Fa503644245fa95201911bfcc85a9%2Fsteinberg-260322-11.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/8615516/2147483647/strip/true/crop/4927x2765+0+260/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F96%2Fc8%2Fa503644245fa95201911bfcc85a9%2Fsteinberg-260322-11.jpg 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/c813d2c/2147483647/strip/true/crop/4927x2765+0+260/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F96%2Fc8%2Fa503644245fa95201911bfcc85a9%2Fsteinberg-260322-11.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="Calbert Wright shows one of reference doors that workers use as a standard for a properly assembled door for the start of their shift at the Ford Chicago Stamping Plant in Chicago Heights Wednesday, March 18, 2026. " srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/c813d2c/2147483647/strip/true/crop/4927x2765+0+260/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F96%2Fc8%2Fa503644245fa95201911bfcc85a9%2Fsteinberg-260322-11.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/ffbdbab/2147483647/strip/true/crop/4927x2765+0+260/resize/980x550!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F96%2Fc8%2Fa503644245fa95201911bfcc85a9%2Fsteinberg-260322-11.jpg 2x" width="490" height="275" data-src="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/c813d2c/2147483647/strip/true/crop/4927x2765+0+260/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F96%2Fc8%2Fa503644245fa95201911bfcc85a9%2Fsteinberg-260322-11.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" > </picture> <div class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Calbert Wright shows one of reference doors that workers use as a standard for a properly assembled door for the start of their shift at the Ford Chicago Stamping Plant in Chicago Heights Wednesday.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Gary Middendorf/For the Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Why did he stay?</p><p>"There weren't jobs paying like this," he said, laughing: $1.40 an hour. "Big money."</p><p>He had a wife, Thelma — now married 65 years — and an infant son to consider. And things were changing.</p><p>"[Martin Luther] King, plus the union, made everybody be classified," Wright said. Conditions improved. He moved up from stacking steel. "That's why I stayed so long."</p><p>Wright's 63-year tenure isn't even the longest of Ford's 177,000 workers — that would be Art Porter, 86, who joined Chicago Stamping in 1961.</p><p>Their longevity is especially amazing when you realize how frequently workers change employers. According to the U.S. Department of Labor, the average worker at a private factory like Ford works 4.9 years before leaving.</p><p>Wright has put in a dozen times that, and seen many changes.</p><p>One of the biggest is automation. When robots were first introduced, in the 1970s, it wasn't clear whether they'd be a benefit.</p><p>"They were throwing parts all over," Wright said. "They were dangerous. They couldn't control it. They were putting welds in the wrong place, blowing holes."</p><h3>Better with robot help</h3><p>Gradually, the machines improved.</p><p>"They got it right now," Wright said. "They come out better with the robots. They put the welds in the same place. When they manpower with a gun, they put one here, one there."</p><p>Walking through the plant with Wright now, it's cool and almost quiet, except for the faint panoply of clanks and hisses. Only occasionally do you spy a person, shielded by machinery.</p><p>"Them robots came in and knocked all those people out," Wright said. "Each line would have 18 people, Now they got three. When I hired in, they had 6,500 people in this plant." </p><p>Now Chicago Stamping employs 1,100.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure — creating doors for Explorers and Lincoln Aviators.</p><p>"I'm a utility man," he said. "You go around the line, instruct people how to do the job. Keep the line running."</p><p>The best way to envision the factory floor is a series of stations, where robots work in a central core, moving like large, jerky birds, grabbing raw steel doors, sending off sheets of sparks as they apply welds affixing window channels, while several workers feed the parts to them. Two buttons control two lights at each station — yellow, signaling the worker needs more parts, and green, signaling repair is required. </p><p>A simple system, but one that has to be followed. This is where Wright comes in.</p><p>"You have to stay up on 'em, because, if they run out of parts, you'd think they'd hit that light?" said Wright. "You're on the line and everything is not cycling. You go up there, 'What's wrong?' [The worker says] "Well, I'm out of parts." [Wright says] "Why don't you hit the lights? The fork driver don't know."</p><p> </p><h3>‘The fun part’</h3><p>Is there a fun part to his job?</p><p>"The fun part..." said Wright. "I go home and say, 'I had a good day.' And got all these rejects, tuck 'em to the side, send them over to salvage. You had a good day."</p><p>He's referring to the detective work aspect to his work. It isn't enough to just pull a flawed part. You have to find out where the dent came from. What's causing it? </p><p>"You gotta find the source," Wright said. "You gotta solve the problem. Track it down from station to station."</p><p>It took three months to figure out what was putting dents into a certain lift gate.</p><p>"They finally caught up with where it was coming from," he said. A plate needed adjustment.</p><p>Machines don't stand up and admit doing something wrong — they're very much like people in that regard. Here Wright uses his experience to counteract the brashness of youngsters, who aren't averse to dropping a connection when called out on a mistake, instead of taking responsibility.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-b30000" name="image-b30000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/5104028/2147483647/strip/true/crop/4402x2471+0+232/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F29%2F2a%2Ff15916a1463eb3fde3dea663eace%2Fsteinberg-260322-09.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/482fe7e/2147483647/strip/true/crop/4402x2471+0+232/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F29%2F2a%2Ff15916a1463eb3fde3dea663eace%2Fsteinberg-260322-09.jpg 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/c28a068/2147483647/strip/true/crop/4402x2471+0+232/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F29%2F2a%2Ff15916a1463eb3fde3dea663eace%2Fsteinberg-260322-09.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="A robotic arm moves a door on the assembly line at the Ford Chicago Stamping Plant in Chicago Heights on Wednesday, March 18, 2026. "Don't tell me your daddy works out front. That don't get you any special privileges on the floor. You have to carry your weight like everybody else."</p><p>Otherwise, the challenge is, "To come in here, and try to run some good parts, and try to get everybody to line up on the same page. A good group will let you know there's something wrong. They love this job."</p><h3>60 years, same workplace</h3><p>Six decades in one factory — what stands out?</p><p>Shortly after he joined, Wright said, a new hire stepped in front of a fork lift carrying a roll of steel — the driver hit the brakes, the steel rolled off the forks and killed him on the spot. He'd been there three days. That taught Wright a valuable lesson.</p><p>"I always been careful when I walk down the aisle," he said. He is surprisingly fit for a man in his mid-80s.</p><p>"I used to go to the gym all the time, LA Fitness, me and my grandson," said Wright.</p><p>His grandson worked in Chicago Stamping for a while, but was killed in a motorcycle accident. "I told him that bike was too fast for him," said Wright, who has seen his share of tragedy. His son also died. But his daughter, Libra, works for the Internal Revenue Service, having gone to Governors State University with lots of support from Ford. "They gave her a lot of money," he said.</p><p>"I said, 'Do better than I did,'" Wright remembered. "Education will get you a chance for advancement."</p><p>He is proud of his two grandchildren, one in the Navy.</p><p>There is also a pride that comes from working for one place so long. The Explorers, for instance.</p><p>"I said, 'This car come out of our plant.' It's beautiful. My daughter got one already."</p><p></p><p>Why does Wright stay? He could be living the life of leisure.</p><p>"To do something, get out of the house," he said. "Otherwise I'd go batty.</p><p>How does he know? Five years ago he took his five weeks of vacation in a single block.</p><p>"I tried it," Wright said. He didn't like it.</p><p>"Sit around, do nothing, the same thing on TV," he scoffed. "Reruns. I get tired of looking at reruns."</p><p>Ford speaks of their employees as family, and sometimes that is literally true.</p><p>"This happens to be my godfather," said Shanetta Gibbs-Cowgur, the United Auto Workers union employee support services programs representative for the plant, whose father Charles worked at Ford Stamping for 31 years. "Before I hired in, he and my dad were friends. It was guys like him who took the younger generation under their wings and showed them about safety, being able to maneuver from Job to job safely."</p><p>Wright lives in Matteson and goes to casinos for fun.</p><p>Looking back over his life, he has no regrets.</p><p>"I could have done a lot of things different," Wright said. "But you can't go back and dream of what you should or could have did. I've been fortunate."</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/columnists/2024/02/27/ford-assembly-plant-chicago-torrence-avenue-100-years-model-t-taurus-explorer" >A century of Ford cars made at Torrence Avenue</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p>

entries.title: Chicago Park District pays more than $2 million to ‘sexually exploited’ lifeguard
entries.summary: <p>The notoriously toxic workplace culture that once festered at Oak Street Beach led the Chicago Park District to pay more than $2 million to a female former lifeguard there — bringing the total legal tab for the sexual-misconduct scandal at the city’s public beaches and pools to more than $8.7 million.</p><p>The alleged misconduct in the case included “grooming, exploitation and sexual assault” by Park District supervisors that began when the plaintiff was still a “minor,” according to court records.</p><p>The recent settlement with the woman, who worked at the popular beach near downtown, marks the seventh legal payout to a former lifeguard since WBEZ first reported on <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/politics/2021/04/27/chicago-park-district-investigating-widespread-sex-abuse-claims" target="_blank" ><u>widespread allegations of sexual abuse</u></a>, assault and harassment in the Park District’s Aquatics Department five years ago.</p><p>Asked about the latest settlement with an unidentified “Jane Doe” plaintiff, a Park District spokeswoman said the agency “considers multiple factors before reaching a settlement agreement and believes the payment is fair and in the best interest of the District.”</p><p>The spokeswoman also said there were no pending court cases and no other unresolved out-of-court claims related to the scandal.</p><p>The total payout in the recently settled case was $2.15 million, according to Park District board meeting records.</p><p>The Chicago law firm of Romanucci & Blandin LLC represented the plaintiff in the case, but a spokeswoman for the firm said the terms of the agreement with the Park District prohibited lawyers from commenting.</p><p>The same firm had won the biggest of the seven settlements related to the lifeguard-abuse scandal for another client. That litigation ended two years ago with the Park District <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/politics/2024/07/30/abused-chicago-lifeguards-receive-more-than-6-5-million-in-legal-settlements" target="_blank" ><u>paying $4 million</u></a> to a woman who alleged abuse by a lifeguard supervisor at Humboldt Park.</p><p>In the case at Oak Street Beach, Cook County Circuit Court records show the plaintiff worked there every summer from 2012 through 2018 and filed the lawsuit in October 2024 against the Park District and its former CEO Michael Kelly.</p><p>The complaint alleged that Kelly and other officials “allowed and concealed a pervasive institutional culture of sexual misconduct directed against female [Park District] lifeguards.”</p><p>The plaintiff became “a victim of [the Park District’s] indifference” — and of senior lifeguards at the iconic beach on Lake Michigan in Chicago’s Gold Coast, according to court records.</p><p>The former lifeguard alleged that the Park District’s leadership “failed to investigate reported sexual abuse at Oak Street Beach” and did not fire or otherwise discipline supervisors who committed sexual misconduct against female employees.</p><p>The case was closed in January, court records show, after the Park District’s board approved the settlement agreement with no dissenting votes. Video from the meeting shows the Park District commissioners did not discuss the matter publicly before approving the settlement.</p><p>The agreement brings the total for the seven payouts to former lifeguards to $8,727,250, according to Park District records obtained by WBEZ.</p><p>In addition to the $4 million case — believed to be the biggest payout by the Park District for any legal matter since at least 2001 — the agency agreed to settlements with two other former Aquatics Department employees in 2024. Those settlements were for $400,000 and $275,000.</p><p>The <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/politics/2023/09/27/chicago-park-districts-big-payouts-to-three-lifeguards" target="_blank" ><u>first three claims</u></a> related to the scandal ended with a settlement for $575,000 in 2022 and payouts of $977,250 and $350,000 in 2023, Park District records show.</p><p>The scandal prompted the <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/politics/2021/12/07/chicago-parks-lifeguard-abuse-investigation-timeline" target="_blank" ><u>resignations of Kelly</u></a>, Park District Inspector General <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/wbez-investigations/2021/09/14/top-watchdog-over-chicago-lifeguard-investigation-resigns" target="_blank" ><u>Elaine Little</u></a>, other high-ranking agency officials and Park District Board President <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/wbez-investigations/2022/06/01/the-former-chicago-parks-leader-blamed-political-pressure-for-her-exit" target="_blank" ><u>Avis LaVelle</u></a>, with then-Mayor Lori Lightfoot ordering an outside-counsel investigation into the matter.</p><p>The park district watchdog’s office opened its probe in 2020, when two young female former lifeguards sent detailed letters to Lightfoot and Kelly. But the matter remained out of public view for more than a year, until WBEZ reported on what already was a <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/stories/chicago-park-district-investigating-widespread-sex-abuse-claims/dbd56a93-9c80-403d-bb0b-c26ea8b29f24" target="_blank" ><u>“broad investigation”</u></a> in April 2021.</p><p>After the story broke, many former lifeguards came forward and said the <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/politics/2021/06/17/female-ex-lifeguards-describe-deacdes-of-sexual-abuse-at-chicagos-beaches-and-pools" target="_blank" ><u>sexual misconduct was endemic</u></a> at the beaches and pools for generations, with officials accused of failing to follow through on their zero-tolerance promises.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/stories/chicago-park-district-suspends-two-lifeguard-managers/90fdf9c2-b1a2-4e50-bcb8-39a6e3ae340e" target="_blank" ><u>Kelly defended his handling</u></a> of the matter, but <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/politics/2021/08/23/whistleblower-chicago-mayor-should-fire-parks-leaders" target="_blank" ><u>former lifeguards told WBEZ</u></a> they were disappointed by the official response. City Council members <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/politics/2021/10/04/lifeguard-abuse-prompts-calls-for-chicago-parks-ceo-to-resign" target="_blank" ><u>raised concerns</u></a>, and Lightfoot eventually <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/stories/lightfoot-parks-chief-should-lose-job-over-lifeguard-sex-abuse-scandal/c9692289-cb0c-409c-a638-942b729aaeff" target="_blank" ><u>forced Kelly to resign</u></a>.</p><p>The outside counsel’s investigation for the Park District concluded that Kelly knew about the explosive allegations far longer than previously revealed and did nothing to investigate the complaints immediately, contrary to his public assertions.</p><p>The Park District inspector general’s office ultimately found <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/stories/chicago-parks-watchdog-reveals-lifeguard-abuse-findings/d10d4bf4-8e0e-42fc-bfc2-904135d95814" target="_blank" ><u>proof to back up 29 allegations</u></a> against employees in the Aquatics Department, concluding that “bullying, harassing and sexual misconduct flourished and went unchallenged.”</p><p>Officials promised reforms to avoid a repeat of the scandal, and the Park District has <a class="Link" href="https://www.chicagoparkdistrict.com/be-lifeguard" target="_blank" ><u>begun recruiting </u></a>lifeguards for the 2026 season. The next swim test for prospective lifeguards is March 28 at Whitney Young High School.</p><p>The Park District is offering $20.50 an hour for lifeguarding this summer, according to a help-wanted ad.</p><p><i>Dan Mihalopoulos is an investigative reporter for WBEZ.</i><br></p>
